OSHA (and the 22 OSHA-approved "state plans" run by 21 states and Puerto Rico) enforce workplace safety and health standards by inspecting workplaces, citing violations and
proposing penalties. Every inspection is recorded. This notebook uses inspections opened in
federal fiscal years 2015 to 2025 (October 2014 to September 2025), their violations, and the
accident investigations OSHA carries out after deaths and serious injuries. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

The summary tables cover every inspection and violation. The `sample` files hold a 5% random
sample of inspections with all of their violations, for record-level questions.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/us-osha-enforcement/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           guess_max = 100000)
}

summary_tbl <- read_module("tidy", "inspection_summary.csv.gz")   # all inspections, aggregated
standards <- read_module("tidy", "violation_standards.csv.gz")    # all violations, by standard
accidents <- read_module("tidy", "accidents.csv.gz")              # accident investigations
injuries <- read_module("tidy", "accident_injuries.csv.gz")       # injured or killed workers
insp <- read_module("sample", "inspections_sample.csv.gz")        # 5% sample of inspections
viol <- read_module("sample", "violations_sample.csv.gz")         # their violations

# OSHA's own inspection counts leave out cases where no inspection took place
inspected <- filter(summary_tbl, insp_scope != "No inspection")
```

# Part 1. How many inspections?

```{r trend}
by_year <- inspected |>
  group_by(fiscal_year, jurisdiction) |>
  summarise(inspections = sum(inspections), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(by_year, aes(fiscal_year, inspections, colour = jurisdiction)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2025) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "OSHA inspections by fiscal year", x = "Fiscal year", y = "Inspections", colour = NULL)

by_year |> pivot_wider(names_from = jurisdiction, values_from = inspections)
```

**Questions**

1. About how many inspections do federal OSHA and the state plans carry out each year?
2. What happened in fiscal years 2020 and 2021? Why?
3. There are roughly 10 million workplaces in the US. At this rate, about how often would a typical
   workplace be inspected? What does that mean for how OSHA must choose where to go?

**Your answer:**



# Part 2. Why does OSHA inspect?

**Planned** inspections are chosen in advance (for example under emphasis programs for high-hazard
industries); **complaints** come from workers; **referrals** come from other agencies or the media,
including employer reports of severe injuries; **fatality/catastrophe** inspections follow a death
or the hospitalization of three or more workers.

```{r types}
inspected |>
  filter(fiscal_year == 2024) |>
  group_by(jurisdiction, insp_type) |>
  summarise(inspections = sum(inspections), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = inspections / sum(inspections)) |>
  slice_max(inspections, n = 6) |>
  arrange(jurisdiction, desc(inspections))

inspected |>
  filter(fiscal_year == 2024, jurisdiction == "Federal") |>
  group_by(naics_sector) |>
  summarise(inspections = sum(inspections)) |>
  mutate(share = inspections / sum(inspections)) |>
  arrange(desc(inspections)) |>
  head(8)
```

**Questions**

1. What share of federal inspections are planned? What share respond to complaints and referrals?
2. Which industry receives the most federal inspections? Why might OSHA focus on it?
3. A complaint inspection depends on a worker speaking up. Which workers might be least likely to
   complain, and what does that mean for who gets protected?

**Your answer:**



# Part 3. What does OSHA cite?

Standards are identified by their section of the Code of Federal Regulations, for example
`1926.501` (fall protection in construction, 29 CFR 1926.501) or `1910.1200` (hazard communication).

```{r standards}
standards |>
  filter(fiscal_year == 2024, jurisdiction == "Federal") |>
  group_by(section) |>
  summarise(violations = sum(violations), penalty = sum(current_penalty)) |>
  arrange(desc(violations)) |>
  head(10)

standards |>
  filter(jurisdiction == "Federal") |>
  group_by(fiscal_year, viol_type) |>
  summarise(violations = sum(violations), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(fiscal_year, violations, fill = viol_type)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2015:2025) +
  labs(title = "Federal OSHA violations by type", x = "Fiscal year", y = "Violations", fill = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Look up the top five standards. What hazard does each address?
2. Which type of violation is most common? What makes a violation "serious", "willful" or "repeat"?
3. Compare the most-cited standards with the leading causes of death in the CFOI module. Do they
   match?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Penalties

The **initial** penalty is what OSHA proposes; the **current** penalty is what remains after
informal settlement, contest and final orders.

```{r penalties}
viol |>
  filter(viol_type %in% c("Serious", "Willful", "Repeat"), initial_penalty > 0) |>
  group_by(viol_type) |>
  summarise(violations = n(),
            median_initial = median(initial_penalty),
            median_current = median(current_penalty, na.rm = TRUE),
            share_reduced = mean(current_penalty < initial_penalty, na.rm = TRUE))

insp |>
  filter(violations > 0, insp_scope != "No inspection") |>
  mutate(size = cut(employees, c(-Inf, 10, 50, 250, Inf),
                    labels = c("1-10", "11-50", "51-250", "251+"))) |>
  group_by(size) |>
  summarise(inspections = n(), median_current_penalty = median(current_penalty))
```

**Questions**

1. What is the median penalty for a serious violation? How often are penalties reduced, and by how
   much?
2. Do larger employers pay larger penalties? OSHA reduces penalties for small employers. Is that fair?
3. Does a penalty of this size create a strong incentive to prevent injuries? Compare it with the
   cost of a serious injury to an employer.

**Your answer:**



# Part 5. Investigations of deaths and serious injuries

Each accident investigation includes a short narrative.

```{r accidents}
accidents |>
  filter(fatality) |>
  count(fiscal_year, name = "fatality_investigations")

accidents |>
  filter(fatality, fiscal_year == 2024) |>
  count(naics_sector, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8)

# Kinds of fatal events, by year (the injuries table links to accidents by summary_nr)
injuries |>
  filter(degree == "Fatality") |>
  inner_join(select(accidents, summary_nr, fiscal_year), by = "summary_nr") |>
  filter(fiscal_year %in% c(2019, 2021, 2024)) |>
  count(fiscal_year, event_type) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = fiscal_year, values_from = n, names_prefix = "FY") |>
  arrange(desc(FY2021)) |>
  head(6)

# Search the narratives
trench <- accidents |>
  filter(fatality, str_detect(str_to_lower(narrative), "trench|excavation"))
nrow(trench)
set.seed(1)
trench |> slice_sample(n = 3) |> pull(narrative) |> str_trunc(400)
```

**Questions**

1. About how many work-related deaths does OSHA investigate each year? The CFOI counts about 5,000
   deaths a year. Why does OSHA investigate fewer than half?
2. Fatality investigations jumped in fiscal years 2020 and 2021. Which event type rose? What was happening? Why is fiscal year 2025 so low (hint: investigations
   take time to close and enter)?
3. Read three narratives. For each, identify the hazard and one control (using the hierarchy of
   controls) that would have prevented the death.
4. Search the narratives for another hazard of your choice (for example "heat", "forklift" or
   "fell"). How many fatal investigations mention it?

**Your answer:**



# Part 6. Which inspections find violations?

```{r hit-rate}
insp |>
  filter(insp_scope %in% c("Complete", "Partial"), fiscal_year >= 2022) |>
  group_by(jurisdiction, insp_type) |>
  summarise(inspections = n(), with_violations = mean(violations > 0),
            serious_per_inspection = mean(serious), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(inspections >= 100) |>
  arrange(jurisdiction, desc(with_violations))
```

**Questions**

1. Which kinds of inspections most often find violations? Why might complaint or referral
   inspections find more (or fewer) violations than planned ones?
2. Is the share of inspections with violations a good measure of how well OSHA targets its
   inspections? What else would you want to know?
3. The sample is 5% of inspections. Compute a 95% confidence interval for the share of planned
   federal inspections with a violation.

# Part 7. Linking records

The inspection number (`activity_nr`) links inspections, violations and accident investigations,
and appears in other OSHA data (the Severe Injury Reports module, for example).

```{r linking}
fatal_inspections <- insp |>
  filter(insp_type == "Fatality/catastrophe", insp_scope != "No inspection")

fatal_inspections |>
  summarise(inspections = n(), with_violations = mean(violations > 0),
            median_penalty = median(current_penalty))

viol |>
  semi_join(fatal_inspections, by = "activity_nr") |>
  count(section, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(10)

injuries |>
  filter(degree == "Fatality") |>
  count(event_type, sort = TRUE) |>
  head(8)
```

**Questions**

1. After a fatality inspection, what share of employers are cited? Which standards are cited most?
2. If an employer is not cited after a worker's death, what might that mean?
3. Design a study that uses inspection numbers to link Severe Injury Reports to the inspections and
   violations that followed. What question would it answer?

**Your answer:**
